facts.fact: A Vietnamese care article uses the name "Thức ăn khô" for dry food.
A Vietnamese shop writes the term as "cám (thức ăn khô) cho cá cảnh", using "cám" for dry fish food.
The same Vietnamese shop uses the heading "Cám Thức Ăn Khô Cho Cảnh".
Prepared dry foods come as flakes, granules and pellets. Complete ones supply protein, fats, vitamins and minerals.
Some dry foods contain colour enhancers such as shrimp meal, spirulina and astaxanthin.
The shop says dry food ("cám") comes as granules, powder, flakes, sticks, and floating or sinking granules ("hạt, bột, mảnh, que, hạt nổi hoặc chìm"), made for carnivores, herbivores and omnivores.
Dry food is easy to store and carry and keeps a long time. The shop says it suits fish that feed at the top and middle, such as betta (Betta), guppy and neon tetra.
Dry food lets you feed quickly and can be fortified with vitamins and minerals.
"dạng mảnh" (flakes): the shop calls them the most common food people think of when feeding aquarium fish.
"mảnh vụn (flake)" is the name one Vietnamese article uses for flake food.
Flakes float at the surface, then slowly sink to reach fish in midwater and at the bottom. They can be crumbled for fry and nano species.
Flakes are thin and soft, so they can fall apart quickly in water. They suit slow eaters and constant grazers poorly.
"dạng viên" (pellets) contain protein, vegetables, vitamins and minerals. The shop says you can stick pellets to the glass for fish to eat from.
"viên nổi" are floating pellets and "viên chìm" are sinking pellets. The article advises checking whether a food floats or sinks ("độ nổi/chìm") when choosing it.
Pellets come in floating kinds for top-dwelling fish, slow-sinking kinds for midwater fish and sinking kinds for bottom fish. They are firm and do not break up right away.
"Dạng tấm" (wafer) sinks slowly to the bottom and softens, and fish nibble it until it is gone.
Wafers and sticks dissolve slowly, so they suit grazers that nibble over hours. Floating sticks are for surface fish such as oscars, sinking sticks for bottom fish such as plecos.
"dạng bột cho cá con" is a powdered dry food for young fish.
"Thức ăn đông khô" (freeze-dried food) is listed as a dry food that keeps much of its nutritional value.
Freeze-dried foods are usually a single protein such as bloodworms, daphnia, tubifex or brine shrimp. They are almost free of moisture, so they float, and they keep at room temperature.
Signs of spoiled dry food: a rancid smell like old cooking oil or crayons, pieces clumping together from moisture, dull or faded colour-enhancing pellets, and visible mould.
Use floating food for surface feeders and fast-sinking food for bottom dwellers. Match particle size to the mouth, and crush flakes for small-mouthed fish.
Feed adult fish about 3% of body weight daily for maintenance, and fry and fingerlings up to 5%. Flakes weigh much less than pellets.
Feed two to three times a day. A few flakes, granules or pellets per fish is enough, and the fish should eat it all in two minutes or less.
Feed only what fish finish in 2-3 minutes ("trong vòng 2-3 phút"), 1 to 2 times a day depending on species and age.
Feed only what fish eat within 2 to 5 minutes ("2 đến 5 phút").
Feed only what fish eat in two to five minutes, once or twice a day, and remove uneaten food right away.
Pellets that swell when wet can expand in a betta's (Betta) stomach and cause bloating. Soak them first, for about a minute or a couple of minutes.
For bettas (Betta), feed 2-4 pellets 1-2 times daily. The site suggests one fasting day per week.
Soak freeze-dried food to rehydrate it before feeding it to bettas (Betta).
To switch a fish from live or frozen food to dry food, mix dry food into its preferred food and raise the dry share gradually.
Freeze-dried, frozen and live foods are not nutritionally complete. Offer them as treats once or twice a week, and only when the water is at least 65 F.
Fish feeds are high in protein and oil and can deteriorate fast. Keep dry feed in a pest-proof container in a cool, dry place, because heat and humidity cause breakdown, mould and rancidity.
Discard an opened container kept at room temperature after 2 months, and commercial feeds kept in the freezer after 6 months.
Use prepared foods within the first six months after opening. Wet fingers, trapped air and open containers degrade them.
Store dry food somewhere dry and airy, out of direct light ("nơi khô ráo, thoáng mát, tránh ánh sáng trực tiếp"). Use packaged food within about 2-3 months of opening.
Vitamin loss starts when a package is opened. After a few months, barely any vitamin C is left.
Flakes lose vitamin C faster than any other fish food because of their high surface-to-mass ratio.
Store food in a sealed container such as a mason jar or screw-top container, in a cool, dark pantry or closet, out of direct sunlight.
Freezing extends the shelf life of many feeds. Thawed feed should not be refrozen.

In humid tropical Singapore (75-90% relative humidity), an open container loses about 50% of its vitamin C in 8-12 weeks. The same container might last about six months in a cool, dry country. This applies to similar humid tropical climates.
In tropical humidity, opened dry food lasts 2-3 months before its vitamins degrade. Unopened dry food lasts 18-24 months if kept cool and dry.
In humid climates, do not keep fish food above the tank, on a windowsill, in a bathroom cabinet, or in its original foil pack after opening.
In humid climates, keep a small daily portion in an airtight jar with a silica pack and freeze the rest in sealed bags. Let a frozen bag warm about 15 minutes before opening it to avoid condensation.
Freeze-dried food absorbs moisture from the air and can mould quickly. Mycotoxins can form before mould is visible.
Overfeeding is much more common than underfeeding. It causes incomplete digestion and more waste, and with uneaten food it pollutes the water.
Overfeeding pollutes the tank and can make fish sick ("Cho ăn quá nhiều có thể làm ô nhiễm bể cá").
Overfeeding can cause obesity, swim bladder disorders, constipation and poor water quality.
Following the can's advice of as much as a betta (Betta) eats in 5 minutes leads to overfeeding. A betta's stomach is roughly the size of its eye.
Pellets that are too large are a mistake. A betta (Betta) that keeps taking and spitting out food may have pellets too big to swallow.
Feeding only dry food for a long time without fresh food may leave fish short of natural enzymes and micronutrients.
Rancid feed is listed as a cause of hepatic lipidosis, a common problem in captive fish.
Buying food for its packaging instead of for whether the species will eat it is a common mistake.
Goldfish (Carassius) with buoyancy disorders need sinking pellets.
PetMD's vet author says flakes can lose up to 90% of their vitamins within 30 seconds in water, and that pellets keep their vitamins longer.
Most feeds should be supplemented with a stabilized form of vitamin C. Too little vitamin C can cause "broken back disease", a severe scoliosis.
Tetra calls TetraMin Flakes a complete food that gives a full diet for the daily feeding of all ornamental fish.
Tetra calls Tetra Phyll Flakes a complete food with plant ingredients, a balanced flake food giving a complete diet for the daily feeding of all ornamental fish.

sera labels sera GVG Mix Royal Flakes a complete feed for all ornamental fish. It describes staple foods as universal foods that can be fed daily and supply all important nutrients in sufficient amounts.
sera's instructions for sera GVG Mix Royal Flakes: feed once or twice daily, only as much as the fish take up within a short time.
UK Pet Food says a good-quality prepared food will give fish a complete and balanced diet with all the nutrients they need.
UK Pet Food advises feeding fish two to three times daily, a few flakes, granules or pellets per fish.
UK Pet Food warns that unless a tank holds only one species, different foods will very likely be needed, so one complete food may not suit every fish in a community tank.
A vet writing for PetMD says most pet fish thrive on a pelleted or flake-based staple diet.
PetMD's vet says live, freeze-dried and frozen foods are not nutritionally complete. They should only complement a pelleted diet and not be the only food unless a vet says so.
None of the maker pages found (Tetra, sera) say outright that their complete food should be the fish's only food. They say it is a complete or full diet for daily feeding.

JBL, the food maker, says in its own words that in a community aquarium "feeding ONE main food is definitely not enough!" Herbivores and carnivores need different foods, so a single product can suit one group and harm the other.
Aquariadise says to keep packs of fish food "well-sealed in a cool, dry, darkened closet", and that flake foods should be "tightly sealed between feeding".
The Vietnamese aquarium shop Aquarium Care calls dry pellet food "cám", for example: "Cám Thái Inve 5/8 hạt nhỏ là một loại thức ăn phù hợp cho rất nhiều loại cá cảnh, từ cá nhỏ đến cá trưởng thành."
Flakes float at first and then sink slowly, so surface and mid-water fish can both reach them.
Flakes are thin, dried pieces that float briefly before slowly sinking.
Flake food can be crushed to match the size of the fry.
Pellets are compressed cylinders or spheres. They are denser than flakes and break down more slowly.
Some pellets, such as Hikari Micro Pellets, float for a short time and then sink slowly, so both surface and mid-water feeders can eat them.
sera Cichlid Sticks are floating sticks that keep their shape and do not cloud the water. They are made for larger cichlids and other large fish.
Tetra Micro Sticks float and then sink slowly. They are meant for small fish that feed in the top and middle of the water, and they soften quickly so fish can eat them easily.
Wafers sink to the bottom right away and slowly soften.
A wafer is not eaten in one bite. It breaks up as the fish nibble at it.
Wafers sink and keep their shape. They suit algae eaters and plecos.
Powdered food is ultra-fine and best for newly hatched fish.
Freeze-dried foods include bloodworms, brine shrimp, daphnia and tubifex. Freeze-drying removes their moisture but keeps their nutrition and taste.
Freeze-dried food floats until it has soaked up water.
Dry food is convenient, keeps for months on the shelf and is easy to portion.
Flake foods are easy to keep and have fairly long shelf lives.
Freeze-dried foods are convenient: they have a long shelf life, are easy to handle and need no refrigeration.
A Vietnamese aquarium site says these fish feeds (cám) can usually be used for a long time and stored safely and cleanly.
